alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic καί ('and'); the Vulgate restructures as a relative-temporal periphrasis Qui cum ('Who, when...'), a typical Latin subordinating idiom replacing Greek parataxis. The Peshitta retains the coordinating ܘ- prefixed to the verb.

Greek uses the aorist participle ἀκούσας ('having heard'); the Peshitta prefixes ܘ- to the perfect ܫܡܥ ('and he heard'); the Vulgate employs the pluperfect subjunctive audisset within the cum-clause. All express the prior act of hearing but with differing aspectual constructions.
ὅτι / ܕ- / quia — the recitative/declarative complementiser.

Greek uses an articular appositive ὁ Ναζαρηνός ('the Nazarene'); the Peshitta supplies the pronoun ܗܘ plus ܢܨܪܝܐ ('he is the Nazarene'), making the copula explicit; the Vulgate gives the bare adjective Nazarenus. The variation is purely syntactic, not semantic.
Greek ἐστιν and Latin est both render the explicit copula 'is'; Syriac expresses the predication enclitically via ܗܘ (grouped above), so no separate copula token is present in the Peshitta.
λέγειν / ܠܡܐܡܪ / dicere — 'to say'; the Vulgate's colon (idx 11) marks the onset of direct speech.

Greek prefaces the vocative with the article ὁ υἱὲ Δαυίδ; the Peshitta uses the bound construct ܒܪܗ ܕܕܘܝܕ ('son of David') with the resumptive 3ms suffix typical of Syriac genitive periphrasis; the Vulgate gives the plain vocative fili David. The Greek and Latin place 'Son of David' before the name 'Jesus', whereas usage of the vocative ordering varies — see next group.

Both Greek and Vulgate include the vocative 'Jesus' (Ἰησοῦ / Jesu), but the Greek places it after 'Son of David' while the Vulgate places it before; the Peshitta omits the address 'Jesus' here, having already named him in the preceding clause.
με / ܥܠܝ / mei — 'on me'; Greek uses the accusative object, Syriac and Latin a prepositional/genitive complement, but the sense is identical.
